analysis.one_liner: Requires businesses to let customers cancel subscriptions the same way they signed up.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote and without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring any company selling a subscription service—magazines, gyms, phone plans, anything with recurring charges—to let customers cancel by the same means they used to sign up. If you could subscribe with one click online, you would have to be able to cancel online too. It never got a hearing or a vote: the House Energy and Commerce Committee took no action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who sign up for recurring-fee services. Companies often make signing up effortless—one click, one phone call—while making cancellation require a letter, a phone call during business hours, or repeated visits, and people keep getting charged for services they meant to stop. The bill would have shifted that burden back to the seller. Anyone who has kept paying for a subscription they tried and failed to cancel would have benefited.

how_it_helps.text: The FTC would have been required, within 180 days of enactment, to issue rules mandating that subscribers be able to cancel a service the same way and by the same means they subscribed to it.
The requirement covered any service with recurring charges, including regular product deliveries, so it applied broadly to subscription businesses rather than one industry.
Ending hard-to-cancel subscriptions stops recurring charges people no longer want, putting a stop to a well-known consumer annoyance rather than a large financial loss per person.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that profit from subscribers who struggle to cancel, and that would have borne the cost of building symmetric cancellation channels—online cancellation systems, self-service portals—and of losing revenue from customers who currently stay subscribed only because quitting is difficult.

drawbacks.text: The bill gave the FTC a single broad mandate without specifying exemptions, so even small businesses selling simple recurring services would have faced rulemaking compliance costs, an objection an honest supporter would have had to address.

The rulemaking route meant the practical protections depended entirely on how the FTC wrote and enforced its rules, so the benefit to consumers was indirect and could have taken years to reach people even if the bill had passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but modest for most households—ending unwanted recurring charges—while the compliance cost falls on sellers, many of whom already offer online cancellation. It was a narrow, low-cost consumer protection rather than a sweeping economic measure, and its main weakness was drafting vagueness, not substance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Zoe Lofgren introduced the Consumer Cancellation Fairness Act on April 25, 2006.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, which is where its consideration ended.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee held no hearing, marked it up, or scheduled a vote, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subscription businesses that rely on hard-to-cancel recurring charges are better off because the bill never advanced; consumers who want to quit such services lost the protection the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it upon introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, markup, or vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes occurred and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Subscription businesses (publishers, gyms, telecom and other recurring-fee sellers)
industries.note: The bill would have required symmetric cancellation—quit as easily as you signed up—ending a common practice of making sign-up effortless and cancellation burdensome. Revenue from subscribers who stay only because quitting is hard would have been at risk.
The bill would have handed the FTC a mandatory rulemaking job and enforcement responsibility, expanding its workload and authority over consumer subscriptions.
